entries.title: Do genes decide exactly how tall you will be?
entries.answer: One gene cannot tell you exactly how tall you will become. Lots of small differences in inherited information can influence how a person grows. Food, health, and other parts of life during childhood can also make a difference. Siblings can inherit different sets of information from the same biological parents and grow to different heights. People also grow at different times. The order of heights among classmates today may look different after everyone has finished growing.
facts: Many different places in DNA influence height.

entries.title: Do your cells have DNA outside the nucleus?
entries.answer: Most of the DNA in a body cell stays in the nucleus. There is also a small amount in some little cell parts called mitochondria. These parts help the cell make energy available for use. Their DNA carries information used there. The way people usually inherit this smaller set is also different. It is usually passed through the biological mother, while the larger sets of chromosomes in the nucleus usually come from both biological parents.
facts: Scientists often shorten mitochondrial DNA to mtDNA.

entries.title: How can people have different versions of a gene?
entries.answer: Imagine looking up the same short passage in two copies of a book and finding a letter that is different. A related thing can happen in DNA. At a certain place, one person may carry a slightly different version from another person. Scientists call each version at that place an allele. Some differences can affect a trait, while others have little or no effect you can see. Often, more than one place in the DNA matters for the same trait.
facts: A difference can be as small as one letter in a stretch of DNA.

entries.title: How do chromosomes help pack DNA?
entries.answer: DNA is long and thin, and a cell is tiny. To pack DNA into that small space, the cell winds it around proteins and folds it further. A piece of DNA and the proteins that help pack it form a chromosome. Chromosomes are especially easy to tell apart after they tighten up as a cell gets ready to divide. Many of your cells have two sets, with one set inherited from each biological parent.
facts: A typical human body cell with a nucleus has 23 pairs of chromosomes.

entries.title: How does one cell become two?
entries.answer: As you grow, the number of cells in your body goes up. One way it happens is that a cell copies its DNA and gets the two matching sets ready to move apart. In a process called mitosis, those sets move into two separate groups. The first cell then splits, leaving two cells with a set of instructions each. The body can use this process to grow and to replace worn cells. Some parts of the body replace cells much faster than others.
facts: Cells copy their DNA before making two cells in this kind of division.

entries.title: What are mitochondria?
entries.answer: In many of your cells are small parts called mitochondria. They help turn energy from food into a form other parts of the cell can use. A muscle cell needs a strong supply when it works, and its mitochondria help provide that supply. The parts are often shown as shapes with folds inside. They even have a little of their own DNA, although most of a person’s DNA is kept elsewhere in cells.
facts: Muscle cells have a need for many supplies of usable energy.

entries.title: What are traits?
entries.answer: A trait is something you can notice or measure about a living thing. The color of a flower and a person’s height are examples. Information you inherit can help shape many traits, but what happens as you grow can matter too. A plant with the same inherited directions may grow differently in a sunny place than in a dark one. Your ability to read a particular book also depends on learning, even though your body has traits that help you see or hear.
facts: A change in a person’s surroundings or experiences can affect some traits.

entries.title: What holds the inside of a cell together?
entries.answer: The outer surface of a human cell is a very thin layer called its membrane. It separates the watery inside from the area around the cell. It also helps control what goes in and out. Some materials can pass through the thin layer. Others need help getting across. The membrane is more than a bag for holding things. It helps a cell get what it needs while keeping its inside different from the place around it.
facts: The cell membrane can help control which materials pass through it.

entries.title: What is a cell in your body?
entries.answer: Your body is built from tiny living units called cells. Most are too small to see without a tool that makes them look bigger. Different cells do different work. A nerve cell can carry a message over a distance, and some muscle cells can shorten when called on to move you. Cells are grouped together into tissues. Several tissues can work together in an organ, which is how small living parts help a body do large jobs.
facts: Examples of human cells include nerve cells, skin cells, and muscle cells.

entries.title: What is a gene?
entries.answer: A gene is a stretch of DNA that carries information a cell can use. Many genes have directions for making a protein, such as one that forms part of a cell or helps it do a job. Some genes help in other ways. A cell does not need to use every gene all the time. A muscle cell and a skin cell can turn to different directions. That can help explain why they do different work even though they both belong to you.
facts: Some genes help a cell make a protein, and some have other jobs.

entries.title: What is a genome?
entries.answer: The full collection of inherited instructions in a living thing is its genome. If you think of a gene as one passage in a big set of books, the genome is the full set. Some parts give information for making proteins. Other parts help run and organize the collection. Plants, animals, and other living things each have genomes. Two people have very similar human genomes, though there can be many small differences between their versions.
facts: A genome can contain information besides the parts that give instructions for proteins.

entries.title: What is DNA?
entries.answer: Many of your cells hold a long, thin material called DNA. Its smaller parts can be thought of as four kinds of letters. The order of those parts carries information. Some stretches help tell cells how to make materials they need, and some help control when instructions are used. Much of your DNA contains information you inherited from your biological parents. The thread is so fine that you cannot see a single strand just by looking.
facts: Your DNA uses four kinds of chemical letters.

entries.title: What is the nucleus of a cell?
entries.answer: Many of the cells in your body have a small part called the nucleus. It has its own border inside the cell. Most of that cell’s DNA is kept there. The cell can use information from DNA when it needs to make materials or get ready to divide. Different kinds of cells use different portions of the information. A cell in your skin can do a different job from one in your muscle even though they hold much of the same DNA.
facts: Most of the DNA in a human body cell is usually in its nucleus.

entries.title: What makes some twins identical?
entries.answer: Identical twins come from one fertilized egg that begins developing and divides into two groups of cells. This gives them almost the same DNA from the beginning. They may look a lot alike and can still be different because each grows and has individual experiences. Fraternal twins start from two separate eggs joined separately with sperm, so each begins with a different mixture of family DNA. They are related in the ordinary way full brothers or sisters are, even though they are born around the same time.
facts: Fraternal twins start from two different fertilized eggs.

entries.title: Why is DNA compared to a twisted ladder?
entries.answer: Think of a ladder with two long sides and rungs in between. A DNA molecule has two sides made of repeating parts. Each rung is a pair of smaller pieces. A piece called A pairs with T, and G pairs with C. The whole ladder coils around itself, so it looks twisted. That shape helps explain how one side of DNA can help a cell work out what belongs on the other side.
facts: The inside pairs use four kinds of units that scientists call A, T, G, and C.
